articles.body: TL;DR The MotoKey Plus app turns Motorola’s AI key into a fully customizable shortcut button with separate actions for single press, double press, and press-and-hold. You can assign useful everyday actions such as the flashlight, screenshots, media controls, notifications, Quick Settings, Gemini, or remap it to launch virtually any app. The app is still unofficial and sideload-only for now, though the developer says a Google Play release is planned. Motorola has been quietly giving Android fans more reasons to pay attention lately, from a cleaner software experience and longer support promises to its upcoming embrace of GrapheneOS . But one part of the experience still feels unnecessarily locked down: the dedicated AI key on some of its phones.

articles.title: A valid webhook signature is not authorization
articles.excerpt: Verifying an HMAC (or other) webhook signature proves the payload came from the vendor. It does not prove which tenant, user, or resource that event is allowed to change in your system. After the sign…
articles.body: Verifying an HMAC (or other) webhook signature proves the payload came from the vendor. It does not prove which tenant, user, or resource that event is allowed to change in your system. After the signature check, map the event to an internal subject and authorize the side effect—create invoice, revoke a seat, mark paid—against that object and tenant, with the same rules you use on your own APIs. A correctly signed body can still carry a spoofed tenant id or an action your customer never granted. Network trust and crypto authenticity are not a policy. Decide subject + action + resource before you mutate state. (Full disclosure, I work with Permit.io.) If you want authorization decisions kept out of ad-hoc webhook glue, Permit.io is one option.

articles.title: Splitting a 2,000-Line automations.yaml into 8 Files
articles.excerpt: My automations.yaml had quietly grown into a 60 KB monster. 2,144 lines. 63 automations stacked end to end in a single file, averaging about 34 lines each. Scrolling it was a chore, editing it made me…
articles.body: My automations.yaml had quietly grown into a 60 KB monster. 2,144 lines. 63 automations stacked end to end in a single file, averaging about 34 lines each. Scrolling it was a chore, editing it made me nervous, and finding one particular heating automation meant a full-text search. The file worked, so there was never any pressure to touch it, and there was a good reason not to: when you refactor a live config you can silently drop the automation that keeps the heating from freezing or the alarm from missing a sensor. So this is a small story about a refactor I almost didn't do, and the one thing that made me trust it: I wrote a 40-line script to split the file, and then I wrote a second, longer script whose only job was to prove the first one hadn't lost anything.

articles.title: Build Secure AI Agents with Microsoft Agent Framework and Auth0
articles.excerpt: A few months ago, I started messing around with Microsoft Agent Framework, and I found it to be very flexible for building AI agents. Like almost everyone, I built a working demo in a short time, but…
articles.body: A few months ago, I started messing around with Microsoft Agent Framework , and I found it to be very flexible for building AI agents. Like almost everyone, I built a working demo in a short time, but then I stopped and thought, " wait, what is this thing actually allowed to do? " Most agent tutorials skip that question entirely. You get a smart chatbot that can search your database, send emails, maybe book a meeting, and the identity story is usually an afterthought. This is not how things work in production. You shouldn't implement an AI agent without stopping to ask who the agent is acting as, what it's allowed to see, or who's responsible when it does something wrong.
articles.author: Andrea Chiarelli

articles.title: even legit coders are being forced to vibe code
articles.excerpt: Something shifted in the last year and I don't think we've named it properly yet. I know a lot of developers. Not Twitter developers, real ones. People who've been writing code for a decade, who read…
articles.body: Something shifted in the last year and I don't think we've named it properly yet. I know a lot of developers. Not Twitter developers, real ones. People who've been writing code for a decade, who read source code for fun, who can debug a memory leak by staring at a heap dump. Serious people. Eighteen months ago they laughed at Copilot. Twelve months ago they tolerated it. Six months ago they started using it quietly. Today some of them are shipping features they don't fully understand, generated by tools they don't fully trust, into codebases they're responsible for, because if they don't, the person next to them will. Nobody says this out loud. Not in standups, not in performance reviews. But it's happening. The pressure isn't coming from managers saying "use AI or else." It's subtler.

articles.title: Hindsight Digital Intelligence
articles.excerpt: A Sales Playbook That Learns From Objections and Outcomes A sales briefing can be wrong while every sentence in it is individually true: the CFO’s objection from one account gets attached to another a…
articles.body: A Sales Playbook That Learns From Objections and Outcomes A sales briefing can be wrong while every sentence in it is individually true: the CFO’s objection from one account gets attached to another account, and a rep walks into the call with someone else’s pricing history. In this project, one field— deal_id —is the difference between useful recall and a confident account mix-up. What it does I built Deal Intelligence Agent as a FastAPI service with three useful API paths. POST /deals/{deal_id}/log retains a call, email, or meeting note in Hindsight Cloud and appends a local copy. GET /deals/{deal_id}/brief recalls one deal’s history and asks Groq’s openai/gpt-oss-120b to produce a structured briefing.

articles.title: How to Evaluate RAG Pipeline Quality: Metrics and Test Harness
articles.excerpt: Most teams building RAG systems spend 90% of their time on retrieval and generation, and 10% on evaluation. That ratio is backwards. Without a rigorous test harness, you're shipping a black box — and…
articles.body: Most teams building RAG systems spend 90% of their time on retrieval and generation, and 10% on evaluation. That ratio is backwards. Without a rigorous test harness, you're shipping a black box — and you'll only find out it's broken when a user does. What You're Actually Measuring A RAG pipeline has two distinct failure modes: retrieval failures (the right context isn't fetched) and generation failures (the model hallucinates or ignores the retrieved context). Your evaluation framework needs to catch both independently. The four metrics that matter in practice: Context Recall : Did the retriever find the documents needed to answer the question? Context Precision : Of what was retrieved, how much was actually relevant?

articles.title: Beyond the Browser: Building Desktop GUI Agents in 2026 with UI-TARS, Claude Computer Use, and OSWorld 2.0
articles.excerpt: Over the past three years, the generative AI ecosystem developed deep specialization in web-browser automation. Tools like Browser-Use, Stagehand, Playwright MCP, and Puppeteer empowered agents to tok…
articles.body: Over the past three years, the generative AI ecosystem developed deep specialization in web-browser automation. Tools like Browser-Use, Stagehand, Playwright MCP, and Puppeteer empowered agents to tokenize Document Object Model (DOM) trees, parse HTML accessibility attributes, and click on Web CSS selectors with remarkable reliability. However, enterprise automation encounters a brutal reality: over 70% of enterprise software workflows do not live inside an open browser DOM . Legacy Enterprise Resource Planning (SAP GUI), native data analytics (Excel workbooks with embedded Visual Basic macros), desktop IDEs, specialized Computer-Aided Design (CAD) applications, terminal shells, and proprietary on-premises clients possess no web DOM.

articles.title: The Job Application Process Is Now Two AIs Lying to Each Other
articles.excerpt: Job applications might be the strangest place AI has taken over. Candidates use it to rewrite resumes and mirror the wording in job descriptions, then have it write the cover letter too. Employers the…
articles.body: Job applications might be the strangest place AI has taken over. Candidates use it to rewrite resumes and mirror the wording in job descriptions, then have it write the cover letter too. Employers then use screening software and AI to work through the growing pile of increasingly polished applications and decide who's worth speaking to. We've built a system where one machine helps a person convince another machine that the person is a person. Nobody involved is being irrational, either. Candidates need to get through automated screening, so they're rewarded for using the right keywords and describing their experience in a language that the system recognises. Employers get more applications than they can reasonably assess by hand, so they add stronger filters.

articles.title: Google is pushing back against opening up Android AI and Search
articles.excerpt: Google would really rather keep the keys to its kingdom.
articles.body: TL;DR Google is challenging the EU’s DMA requirements in court, which would force it to open Android further to rival AI assistants and share Search data with competitors. The Android changes could eventually let you set an AI assistant like ChatGPT as your preferred assistant and summon it with a voice command. Google says the Search requirement could put users’ privacy at risk, arguing that personal search queries could be exposed to rivals without sufficient anonymization and safeguards. Back in July, the European Commission handed Google a pretty big to-do list . It wanted the company to make Android more open to rival AI assistants and separately asked it to share Google Search data with competing search providers.

articles.title: NASA Armstrong Celebrates 80 Years of Flight Innovation
articles.excerpt: On Sept. 30, 1946, five National Advisory Committee of Aeronautics (NACA) engineers arrived at Muroc Army Airfield in California’s high desert to achieve supersonic flight for the first time. In less…
articles.body: On Sept. 30, 1946, five National Advisory Committee of Aeronautics (NACA) engineers arrived at Muroc Army Airfield in California’s high desert to achieve supersonic flight for the first time. In less than two years, NACA flew the X-1 aircraft faster than the speed of sound, marking an important milestone in aviation history. Fast forward 80 years, and that former NACA outpost is now NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, flying the X-59 supersonic X-plane in the same skies to demonstrate that supersonic flight doesn’t have to come with a boom. Over Armstrong’s 80-year history, the center has supported milestone missions ranging from space shuttle landings to SR-71 flights, shaping the evolution of science, aeronautics, and space research.
